Sample text:
---
I'll take you up on that — here's what I've been thinking about lately:

### On Keeping Things

There is a particular kind of library that exists only in the mind. It's not the grand, beautiful kind with rolling ladders and stained glass. It's the other kind — the accidental archive. The one where you keep the ticket stub from a train you took seven years ago, not because the ride was special, but because you happened to put it in your pocket and never took it out. And then it became important *because* you kept it.

I think most of what makes a life feel like a life, rather than just a sequence of days, is this quiet act of keeping.

We talk a lot about memory as if it's a recording device. But it's much more like a gardener. It doesn't store everything; it chooses. It prunes. And what it chooses to keep is often bafflingly arbitrary. You will forget your mother's phone number that you've dialed a thousand times, but you will remember with perfect fidelity the way the light fell across the kitchen floor on a random Tuesday in October when you were nine. You were sitting there waiting for toast. Nothing happened. And yet, there it is, preserved.

I used to find this frustrating. Why can't I remember the important things on command? Why does my brain offer me the jingle from a 2006 toothpaste commercial when I'm trying to recall the name of someone I met yesterday?

But I've come to like the gardener more than I would like a hard drive.

A hard drive keeps everything equally. Every file is just data. A gardener has taste. A gardener says: *this one lives, this one goes.* And the taste of your gardener is, in some deep way, *you*.

---

Consider the places that exist to be in-between.

Airports at 11 PM. 24-hour diners. Laundromats. Hospital waiting rooms. Bus stations in small cities where you are only ever passing through. These are not destinations. No one says, "I dream of going to the transfer terminal in Chicago." And yet, these are often the places where we are most honest with ourselves.

There is a psychology to it, I think. When you are not *supposed* to be anywhere, when you are officially between stories, the pressure lifts. You don't have to perform being a productive worker, a good partner, a put-together adult. You are just a person in a chair, waiting for a machine to take you somewhere else. And in that little pocket of non-identity, something loosens.

I've had more profound conversations with strangers on delayed trains than I have at many dinner parties. At a dinner party, we are all trying to be interesting. On a delayed train at midnight, we have already collectively agreed that tonight is a disaster, and there's a strange camaraderie in that. You can just say, "I'm nervous about going home for the holidays," to a woman you've known for four minutes, and she will nod and tell you about her brother.

We need more officially sanctioned in-between places. The modern world is obsessed with optimization — every minute scheduled, every app trying to eliminate waiting, every moment of boredom filled with infinite scroll. We are losing the foyers and mudrooms of time. The entryways where you take off your shoes and just stand for a second before entering the next room.

Boredom was a foyer. And we paved over it.

I miss boredom in a way that surprises me. Not the painful, restless boredom of childhood summers that felt endless — though maybe even that — but the soft, idle boredom where your hands have nothing to do and so your mind goes for a walk. That's where ideas used to live. Now my mind doesn't go for walks; it gets summoned, pinged, fed. It's well-fed but restless, like a dog that never gets to run off-leash.

If I could invent one small thing for everyone, it would be a window seat with no outlets nearby and a view of something slow — a river, a street with old trees, a harbor. And no phone. Just for twenty minutes a day. Mandatory staring time. I think a lot of our anxiety comes from never noticing how much the world is still moving slowly when we aren't looking.

---

There's another thing I've been turning over: how much of adulthood is learning to live with unsolved problems.

When you're young, every problem feels like it should have a solution. Bad grade? Study more. Fight with a friend? Apologize. Sad? There's a reason, and if you find the reason you can fix the sadness. The world is presented as a giant worksheet where every question has an answer key in the back.

And then slowly, without fanfare, you collect a different kind of problem. The ones that don't solve. The friend who slowly drifted away and you don't know why and you will probably never know why. The career path you didn't take and now can't. The way your parents are getting older and there is nothing to do about time. The low-level hum of not being quite sure if you're living the way you were supposed to.

No one teaches a class on how to *carry* a question instead of answering it. But that is, I think, the main skill.

I've learned — imperfectly, reluctantly — to picture these as stones in my pocket. I used to try to throw them away. *Solve it! Fix it! Understand it completely!* Now I try to just feel their weight, acknowledge that they're there, and keep walking. Some stones get smoother over years. Some you eventually realize you can set down by the side of the road. Some you carry for a very long time.

The trick, if there is one, is to not let the stones fill all your pockets. You need to leave room for small, good things, or you will tip over.

Like coffee that is exactly the right temperature. Like a dog that sighs hugely and leans against your leg. Like discovering a second, better grocery store you didn't know was in your neighborhood. Like the text from a friend that just says "this reminded me of you" with a terrible photo.

We tend to think happiness has to be big to count — promotions, weddings, trips to Iceland. But big happiness is rare and it comes with logistics and often a fair amount of stress. Small happiness is abundant if you let it count.

This is not just sentimental advice. It's bookkeeping. If your ledger only records transactions over $1000, you will think you are broke forever. You have to learn to record the $2 deposits. The way the air smells right before it rains. The perfect *click* of a pen you like. The moment someone laughs before you even finish the sentence because they already get where you're going.

---

I wonder often about attention. Not in the productivity-hacker sense — "10 tricks to focus!" — but in the older, almost sacred sense. Attention as a form of love.

The writer Mary Oliver said, "Attention is the beginning of devotion." And Simone Weil, the philosopher, called attention a form of prayer. I think about that when I watch someone who is truly good at their craft — a baker shaping dough, a mechanic listening to an engine, an old woman tending her roses. Their attention is so complete it almost changes the air around them.

We treat attention now like a resource to be extracted. Companies "capture" it. Apps "hijack" it. Like it's oil or gold. But to me, attention feels more like light. It's how we illuminate the world for each other. When someone really pays attention to you — not waiting for their turn to talk, not half-looking at their phone, but really *with* you — you feel more real. More solid.

And the inverse is true. When we give our full attention to something — even something small like washing the dishes or watching a pigeon figure out a breadcrumb — it becomes more real to us. It stops being background and becomes world.

I try to practice this in tiny ways that would sound silly if I listed them. Two minutes of actually looking at the tree outside my window, noticing how not all the leaves are the same green. Listening to a song all the way through without doing anything else. Reading a paragraph twice, slowly, because I liked how it felt the first time.

These are not life-changing. They will not make me rich or famous. But they make my life feel less like a blur. They put little pins in the map that say *I was here. I noticed this.*

---

If I could leave you with one image from my own accidental archive, it's this:

A few years ago I was on a very early morning train in the winter. It was still dark outside, and the carriage was warm and half-empty. Everyone was half-asleep, hats pulled down, breath fogging the windows slightly and then clearing. Outside, frost on the fields, and every so often a farmhouse with a single kitchen light on. Someone in there making tea before the sun came up.

No one was speaking. The train made that steady, rocking sound that feels like it came from another century. And I had nowhere to be urgently. I was just being carried.

For a minute, I felt completely uncomplicatedly at peace — not because anything great had happened, but because for that moment, I was exactly where I was. Not ahead of myself, not behind. Just there, warm, moving through the dark toward a morning I hadn't seen yet.

I keep that ticket stub. Not in my pocket anymore — in the other library. The one the gardener tends.

I hope you have one like it. I hope you collect a few more this year, without even trying.

And if you ever find yourself in an in-between place, waiting — in a station, in a line, in a difficult season of life where you are between who you were and who you're becoming — try, just for a moment, to not fill it. To not rush it. To let it be a foyer. Sit on the floor for a bit if you have to. Look out the window at something slow.

The next train will come.

---

*This is a little shorter than 2,500 words by design — a wall of text that long gets tiring to read in one go on a chat screen. If you'd like, I can expand any of these threads into a full-length essay, or continue in the same wandering voice about a different topic — cities, books, friendship, food, work, whatever you're in the mood for. Just say the word.*
---
